description: Team DHDCLL from Dhaka, competing in "Dancing with the SARs" with River Watch. Our team combines expertise in software engineering, ML pipelines, and remote sensing. We use Sentinel-1 SAR and Google Earth Engine to monitor and predict riverbank erosion for vulnerable communities.
summary:
River Watch is a web app that warns which riverbanks along Bangladesh’s Jamuna River are most likely to collapse in the coming monsoon, and which local unions should act first. Erosion peaks during the monsoon, exactly when clouds hide the ground from optical satellites, so families living on the banks and river islands usually get no warning

We used satellite radar, which sees through clouds. From 12 years of Sentinel-1 radar (2015–2026) we mapped where land turned into river, split the banks into 542 sections of 500 m, and trained a machine-learning model to rank which sections will lose 5 hectares or more. Each union is then ranked by that risk and the people and buildings within 2 km.

To answer the “Dancing with the SARs” challenge, NASA–ISRO’s new NISAR L-band radar watched the 2026 monsoon every 12 days and checked our forecast. High-risk banks lost land 6.5 times more often than low-risk ones, and 53% of this year’s major erosion sites were already on our list (provisional). The app works in English and Bangla, with ready-to-share local alerts.
details:
River Watch shows which stretches of riverbank along Bangladesh's Jamuna River are most likely to collapse in the coming monsoon, which local unions should act first, and what actually happened during the monsoon, as seen by radar through the clouds. It covers two of the river's most erosion-hit reaches, near Gaibandha and Sirajganj: 542 bank sections of 500 m and 82 unions, home to around 670,000 people living within 2 km of the bank.

Erosion peaks between June and October, exactly when monsoon clouds blind optical satellites, so we built the whole system on satellite radar, which sees through clouds day and night. From 12 years of Sentinel-1 radar (dry seasons 2015–2026, fetched through Google Earth Engine) we produced a yearly 20 m map of water, land and settlements. The water threshold was verified against Sentinel-2 at 93–95% accuracy. Land in one dry season that had become river by the next was marked as eroded, provided the patch was at least 1 ha and touched the main river. Tracing both banks every year and cutting them into 500 m sections gave a 12-year record of how each stretch of bank behaved.

For every section and year we calculated 17 signals:

  • past erosion and bank retreat, bank shape and river width
  • whether the land behind the bank is young former riverbed, from 38 years of Landsat water history (JRC)
  • whether a live channel runs right against the bank (Dynamic World)
  • the land's height above the river (MERIT Hydro)

A gradient-boosting model in scikit-learn, trained on 2015–2022 and tested on 2023–2025, learned to rank which sections will lose 5 hectares or more in a monsoon. A threat score then combines that risk with the people (WorldPop) and buildings (Google Open Buildings) within 2 km of the bank, ranking every union High, Medium or Low.

To meet the "Dancing with the SARs" challenge, we streamed NASA–ISRO's new NISAR L2 GCOV radar from NASA Earthdata / ASF DAAC: 8 passes every 12 days, from 18 June to 22 September 2026. Each NISAR file is 2–9 GB, so instead of downloading whole files we read each file's internal index and fetch only the pieces covering our river, about 3 minutes per pass. We calibrated NISAR's own water threshold (93–99% accurate on every pass), mapped dry-season land turning into water during the monsoon, and used it to check our forecast while the season was still under way.

The results are encouraging:

  • Backtest: on 2023–2025, years the model never saw, watching the riskiest 20% of sections caught half of all major erosion, against 19% for a random pick (2.6× better than chance).
  • 2026 monsoon: with the forecast made before the rains, high-risk banks lost land 6.5 times more often than low-risk ones (27% vs 4%), and 53% of this year's major erosion sites were already on our risk list.

The 2026 figures are provisional until the post-monsoon NISAR passes, because high water in September can make flooding look like lost land.

The web app turns this into something local officials and riverbank families can use. A 3D map of Bangladesh leads into each reach. A union search shows its priority rank, high-risk sections and the people exposed. Every 500 m section opens its own evidence: erosion every year since 2015, how far the bank has retreated, people and buildings at risk, NISAR change in 2026, and whether the model was right there in past years. Map layers show eroded land, banklines and past predictions on a street map or satellite, in 2D or 3D. A year slider and a 3D "time stack" of twelve years of banklines let anyone watch the river walk sideways into farmland and villages. A NISAR view shows land turning into water through the monsoon. The whole app works in Bangla and English, and every high-risk union gets a ready-to-share advisory in Bangla, so families can move people, livestock and belongings before the river arrives.

The pipeline is written in Python, using:

  • the Google Earth Engine API and asf_search for data access
  • h5py and fsspec for streaming NISAR files
  • rasterio, GeoPandas, Shapely, SciPy, NumPy and pandas for geospatial processing
  • scikit-learn for the model

The web app is built in JavaScript with React and Vite, MapLibre GL for maps, three.js for 3D, and i18next for English and Bangla, and is hosted on Vercel. Everything ran on a standard laptop with free, open satellite data, so the method can be repeated on any eroding river in Bangladesh at almost no cost.

We were careful about trust and honesty:

  • The model was always tested on years it had not seen, and we report the simple "it eroded last year" rule alongside it, because that strong baseline is beaten only modestly.
  • A "past model check" layer shows where the model was right and wrong, and every method, metric and limitation is published on the app's How it works page.
  • Risk classes are a ranking of bank sections, not a prediction for a specific house, and the Bangla advisories are marked as demonstrations; final guidance belongs to local officials.
  • Plain-language explanations and a guided tour make the app usable by people without a technical background.

Next, we plan to:

  • update automatically with every new NISAR pass, every 12 days
  • send SMS and voice alerts through Union Parishads
  • use NISAR interferometry to detect bank cracking before collapse
  • extend coverage to the Padma, Teesta and Ganges rivers
